note.text: Prose uses sentences and paragraphs rather than requiring verse lines. Fictional character can be presented directly through description or indirectly through speech, action and others’ responses. Setting includes place, time and social conditions; it can create obstacles and shape choices. A narrator’s viewpoint is not automatically the author’s personal belief. An interpretation should cite a detail and explain its effect.

sections.heading: Your goal and connections
sections.text: By the end, you should be able to explain how an original prose passage presents character through action and setting. Builds on: evidence-based inference. Leads to: creative narrative and drama comparison.

sections.heading: Read the original model
sections.text: Original passage: At the crowded bus shelter, Ngozi kept her folder beneath her jacket. A stranger’s papers scattered into the puddles. She hesitated, shifted her own folder under a dry bench, then knelt to help. The wet crowded setting creates a practical conflict. Her sequence of actions suggests concern for both her own work and another person, without proving an unchanging trait in every situation.

sections.heading: Apply and check
sections.text: Identify a setting detail, a character action and their connection. Explain what the sequence suggests and what remains uncertain. Use this original passage for foundations; no prescribed novel is substituted.

cards.idea: A correction must preserve the intended meaning and form.
example: An action proves the character acts identically forever. Correction: Character interpretation must match the particular evidence.
Setting can never affect a character’s choices. Correction: Conditions can create obstacles and opportunities.
Every narrator is identical to the real author. Correction: A constructed voice and its author are distinct.
A character label needs no quoted or described action. Correction: Evidence connects a reading to the passage.

pick.q: Original prose: Tabe gave his dry seat to a traveller but kept a place for his bag. Which reading is best supported?
pick.r: He offers help while still attending to his belongings
w: He is proved generous in every event of his life
e: The offered seat contradicts total rejection.
The bag is mentioned.
One scene does not prove every future action.
pick.y: Read both actions and limit the conclusion.

pick.q: Original prose: The narrow bridge made the group cross in single file. What does the setting do?
w: Proves the narrator built the bridge
Shows every character has the same motive
e: The builder is not identified.
Motives are not supplied.
The narrowness creates a constraint.
pick.y: Connect physical detail with its effect on the action.

pick.q: Original prose: I thought the locked door was a warning, though I had not asked the caretaker. What should a reader distinguish?
pick.r: The narrator’s interpretation from an established explanation
w: A proven statement by the caretaker
Proof the door was never locked
e: The caretaker has not been asked.
The lock is part of the narrated observation.
The narrator’s belief does not establish authorial intention.
pick.y: A first-person account can reveal a limited viewpoint.
